en.title: Agricultural Extension: the whole course
en.short: What agricultural extension is, how the degree is organised, the main areas, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Agricultural extension is education and advisory work with rural people. It helps farmers, households and groups make informed decisions, solve problems, adopt or adapt practices, and connect with research, markets, inputs and public services. It is not only giving advice. Good extension is two-way: the agent listens, learns from farmers and brings their problems back to researchers and policy makers. The subject draws on agriculture, adult education, communication, sociology, economics and management. Extension agents work for government services, NGOs, private companies, cooperatives and projects. The same principles apply in Africa, Asia and elsewhere, though the institutions and policies differ by country.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Degrees differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, agricultural extension is usually studied within a Faculty of Agriculture, often as B Agriculture or BSc Agricultural Extension and Rural Development. A first degree commonly takes four to five years, depending on the programme and university. Programmes follow benchmarks from the National Universities Commission; polytechnics under the National Board for Technical Education award ND and HND in agricultural technology and related fields, and colleges of education award the NCE. Field attachment, often called SIWES, is part of many programmes. Postgraduate study leads to MSc and PhD degrees, with a thesis or dissertation.

In the United Kingdom, agriculture and rural business degrees commonly take three years and may include extension or advisory modules; a master’s usually takes one year. In Kenya and Ghana, BSc agriculture programmes commonly take four years. Award titles, course codes and compulsory field work vary, so confirm the current rules with your department.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually starts with foundations. You learn the meaning, history and principles of extension; its philosophy, objectives and scope; extension systems, institutions and agents; rural society and farm households; rural livelihoods, poverty and food security; agricultural systems and production basics; communication; teaching and learning; and the mathematics and statistics needed for surveys, records and evaluation.

The core follows. It covers diffusion of innovations and adoption; extension models and approaches; methods and media; teaching aids and message design; programme planning; management and administration; monitoring and evaluation; participatory rural appraisal; farmer field schools and experiential learning; research, extension and input supply linkages; technology generation, transfer and adaptation; gender, youth and social inclusion; farmer organisations and cooperatives; agribusiness, value chains and market linkages; farm management and enterprise budgeting; farm records and accounts; economics and financing of extension; ICT in extension; climate-smart advisory services; research methods; professional ethics; and a project, field attachment and report.

Master’s level deepens theory and policy, agricultural innovation systems and scaling, and advanced research methods leading to a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study with real farms and real people in mind. After each topic, write a short definition in your own words and give one local example. For quantitative topics, practise the calculations: survey percentages, averages, enterprise budgets, gross margins, records and evaluation indicators. Check every answer against the original figures.

Visit a farm, a cooperative or an extension office if you can. Observe how messages are delivered and how farmers respond. Read your country’s current agricultural extension policy and the annual reports of a public extension service. Keep a glossary of terms such as adoption, diffusion, participatory appraisal and monitoring. Learn to write short, clear reports, because extension work depends on communication.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Common mistakes include treating extension as one-way advice, ignoring farmers’ knowledge, and assuming that adoption means impact. Students often confuse a survey with an experiment, choose samples carelessly, or report correlation as causation. They define indicators after collecting data, or copy a foreign model without checking local conditions. Many forget gender, youth and social inclusion, or make promises about inputs and prices that the service cannot keep.

Other errors are poor farm records, budgets that omit a cost, and reports that hide failures. Ethical conduct matters: ask permission, protect personal data, and do not raise expectations you cannot meet. Always state the country, year and source of any rule or statistic you quote.

keyPoints: Agricultural extension is two-way education and advisory work that helps rural people make informed decisions and solve problems.
Extension draws on agriculture, communication, adult learning, economics and social science.
Degree length, awards and field requirements differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Learn the foundations first, then core methods, planning, evaluation and specialised advisory areas.
Practise calculations and field observation; clear records and reports are part of the work.
Avoid one-way advice, weak sampling, unclear indicators and promises that cannot be kept.

en.title: Meaning, History and Principles of Agricultural Extension
en.short: What extension is, how it differs from research and teaching, and its historical models.

sections.heading: Definition and boundaries
sections.text:
Agricultural extension is non-formal education and advisory support that helps farm households and rural people make informed decisions, solve problems and adopt or adapt practices. It is voluntary, practical and field-based, and it carries farmers’ problems back to research and policy.

Extension is not research. Research generates and tests knowledge; extension helps farmers judge, adapt and use it. It is not formal teaching, which leads to certificates; extension is adult learning in fields and homes. Advisory work is narrower: expert advice on specific problems. Extension includes advice but adds group learning, organisation and feedback.

sections.heading: Principles
sections.text: Principles include starting from farmers’ real problems, involving them in planning, two-way communication, using local leaders and groups, keeping advice practical and locally relevant, working with the whole farm and household, cooperating with other agencies, and remaining accountable. Participation should be voluntary, and advice should respect local knowledge.

sections.heading: Historical growth
sections.text:
Colonial departments of agriculture in Africa and Asia often ran demonstration plots and model farms, mainly for export crops. After independence, many countries expanded public extension, often supply-driven (agents delivered what officials chose, not what farmers asked for). In the 1970s and 1980s the World Bank promoted training and visit (T&V): regular agent visits to contact farmers (selected farmers expected to pass messages on to neighbours), with supervisors and close research links. T&V raised yields where inputs and transport existed, but was costly elsewhere.

Farmer field schools (FFS) grew from integrated pest management work in Indonesia in the late 1980s. Farmers met weekly through a season, observed fields, tested options and learned by discovery. Since the 1980s and 1990s, pluralistic advisory systems have spread: public agencies, NGOs, private firms, input dealers, farmer organisations and ICT services all provide advice. No single model fits every country.

sections.heading: Illustrative case
sections.text: Consider a fictional case. Amina grows maize in Kano State, Nigeria. An agent demonstrates a new variety on her farm. Amina compares it with her own seed, records the result and discusses it with a group. The agent reports her questions to researchers. This is extension: joint learning and feedback, not a lecture.

keyPoints: Agricultural extension is voluntary, non-formal education and advisory support that helps rural people make informed decisions.
Research generates and tests knowledge; extension helps farmers judge, adapt and use it, while formal teaching leads to qualifications.
Extension principles include starting from farmers’ problems, two-way communication, local relevance and accountability.
Training and visit (T&V) used regular agent visits and contact farmers; it worked where inputs and transport existed but was costly.
Farmer field schools use season-long, field-based group discovery learning.
Pluralistic advisory systems involve public, private, NGO, farmer organisation and ICT providers, and no single model fits all.

en.title: Philosophy, Objectives and Scope of Agricultural Extension
en.short: Why extension exists, its goals, and how public, private and NGO objectives and scope differ.

sections.heading: Why extension exists
sections.text: Extension is informal education and advice that helps rural people make informed decisions. Its philosophy is farmer-centred and voluntary: people are not ordered to change. The adviser listens, teaches, demonstrates and links farmers to knowledge and services. Extension exists because research, markets and policy produce information farmers need, while farmers hold local knowledge that researchers and planners need. The aim is to help people help themselves, not to create dependence.

sections.heading: Goals it pursues
sections.text: Extension pursues several goals. Higher productivity means more output from the same land, labour or capital. Better food security means reliable availability of, access to and use of safe, nutritious food. Improved rural livelihoods means higher, more stable incomes and less risk. Stronger farmer organisations means groups that share information, buy and sell together, and speak to government and markets. The goals can conflict: a push for output may favour larger farmers, while inclusion may need extra effort with poorer households. Good extension states its priorities openly.

sections.heading: Objectives and scope
sections.text:
Objectives differ by employer. Public extension is usually government-funded and serves public goals: national food security, rural welfare, smallholder support and safe practice. Private advisory services, such as input suppliers or processors, serve business goals: profitable clients, reliable supply, product sales and quality standards. NGO extension usually serves poverty reduction, empowerment, inclusion and sustainability, often with project funding. These are typical patterns, not fixed rules; objectives overlap.

Scope is the range of work expected. It may cover crops, livestock, farm management, marketing, nutrition, climate risk and group development, and link farmers to research, credit, inputs and markets. Scope varies by country, mandate and budget. In a rice area in Kebbi State, Nigeria, a public adviser might teach spacing to all farmers, a private seed adviser promotes certified seed, and a rice processor buys paddy (unhusked rice), while an NGO adviser helps women’s groups with savings and collective marketing.

keyPoints: Extension is voluntary, farmer-centred education, not coercion.
Its goals include productivity, food security, rural livelihoods and stronger farmer organisations.
Public extension usually serves public goals and smallholder welfare.
Private advisory services usually serve business and market goals.
NGO extension usually serves poverty reduction, inclusion and sustainability.
Scope varies by country and mandate; extension links farmers to services but cannot replace them.

en.title: Extension Systems, Institutions and Agents
en.short: How national extension systems are structured and how public, private and farmer agents deliver advice.

sections.heading: Public system structure
sections.text: A national extension system is the network of organisations, people and policies that link research and policy to farmers. Structures differ by country, but many have a ministry of agriculture that sets policy, a public extension service that employs field agents, research institutes that generate technology, and local government units that manage or support staff. Services are often arranged in tiers: national, regional or state, district and village. The exact division of duties varies, so check the current law and official guidelines for the country concerned.

sections.heading: Universities and private agents
sections.text: Universities train extension workers and conduct research; some also run advisory clinics or farm helplines. Agro-dealers sell seed, fertiliser and pesticides and often give advice; because they profit from sales, they need training and their advice needs regulation. NGOs run projects, sometimes with donor money, and may reach remote or poorer groups, but services can stop when a project ends. Farmer groups and cooperatives share information, buy inputs and market produce. Lead farmers are selected farmers who demonstrate good practice and advise neighbours. They are useful, but need training, support and a clear link to qualified agents.

sections.heading: Delivery models
sections.text: Centralised delivery means a national ministry controls budget, staff and rules. It gives uniform messages and is easier to coordinate, but can be slow and poorly fitted to local needs. Decentralised delivery gives authority to regional or local government. It is more responsive, but capacity and funding vary between areas. Pluralistic delivery uses several providers: public services, private firms, NGOs and farmer organisations. It widens reach and choice, but needs coordination, quality control and clear roles. A country may combine all three.

sections.heading: Case and coordination
sections.text: In a district, a public agent coordinates. A university tests soil, an agro-dealer supplies certified seed, an NGO trains a women’s group, and a lead farmer hosts a field day. A committee meets to avoid conflicting advice.

keyPoints: National extension systems usually link policy, research, public services and local government, but structures vary by country.
Universities train staff and do research; agro-dealers sell inputs and advise, so their advice needs regulation.
NGOs and farmer groups widen reach but may be project-bound or need support.
Lead farmers demonstrate practices and advise neighbours but do not replace trained agents.
Centralised models are uniform and easier to coordinate; decentralised models are more local but uneven.
Pluralistic models use many providers and need coordination, quality control and clear roles.

en.title: Rural Society and Farm Households
en.short: Covers rural social structure, kinship, class, migration, farm households, decisions, labour and gender roles.

sections.heading: Rural social structure
sections.text: Rural society is not a uniform group. It is households and communities linked by kinship, residence, land, occupation and local institutions. Social structure is the settled pattern of these links: who holds authority, who uses land, who shares labour and who joins groups. A farm household shares a home, food or farm enterprise. It is not always a parent-and-children family; it may include grandparents, married sons, orphans, workers or absent migrants. Extension works with this real group.

sections.heading: Kinship and class
sections.text: Kinship is relationship by blood, marriage or adoption. It creates duties and claims: help at harvest, care for elders, access to land through inheritance and support in sickness. Class means unequal access to land, livestock, education, cash and influence. A landholder, a tenant and a landless labourer share a village but face different risks and needs. Do not treat a village as one audience. Ask who speaks, who owns what and who is excluded.

sections.heading: Migration and household
sections.text: Migration is movement to live or work elsewhere. It may be seasonal, circular or long-term, and rural-urban or rural-rural. Migrants may send remittances, money sent home, to pay for inputs, school fees or food. Migration can remove young labour at peak seasons and leave women, older people or children managing farms. Household make-up changes over the year. Extension should record who is present and who decides when a migrant is away.

sections.heading: Decisions and gender
sections.text: Household decision making is shared and contested, not one head deciding all. Members bargain using income, land rights, knowledge and standing. Labour allocation means choosing how family, hired and shared labour are used across crops, livestock, home work and off-farm jobs. Gender roles are tasks and rights society assigns to women and men; they vary by place. In one case, Aisha and Musa farm in northern Nigeria. Musa grows maize; Aisha keeps goats and sells vegetables. An agent visiting only Musa misses Aisha’s choices on goat health and vegetable sales. Visit both and ask who controls the income.

keyPoints: Rural social structure is the pattern of authority, land use, labour sharing and group membership in a community.
Kinship creates rights and duties that shape access to land, labour and support.
Class differences in land, income, education and influence mean a village is not one audience.
Migration changes household make-up and labour, and remittances can fund farming.
Household decisions are shared and contested, so extension should ask who decides and who controls income.
Gender roles in farming vary by place; visit both women and men and avoid assuming the male head speaks for all.

en.title: Rural Livelihoods, Poverty and Food Security
en.short: The sustainable livelihoods framework, poverty and food security, and how extension affects poor farmers’ options.

sections.heading: Livelihoods and assets
sections.text:
A livelihood is how a person or household makes a living: the assets used, activities done and risks faced. The sustainable livelihoods framework helps extension workers see these links. It groups assets into five capitals. Human capital is health, knowledge and skills. Natural capital is land, water, trees and soil. Physical capital is tools, livestock, roads and stores. Financial capital is cash, savings and credit. Social capital is trust, networks and groups.

The framework also considers vulnerability (drought, price shocks, illness), institutions and rules, livelihood strategies and outcomes. Households often combine crops, livestock and trading.

sections.heading: Poverty and food security
sections.text:
Poverty is more than low income. It is a lack of access to basic needs and opportunities, such as food, shelter, health care, education and a voice in decisions. National poverty lines differ by country and year, so check current official figures. Food security exists when all people, at all times, have physical, social and economic access to enough safe and nutritious food for an active and healthy life. Its pillars are availability, access, utilisation and stability.

A household may live near markets yet be food insecure if it lacks money or control over land. Food insecurity may be chronic or temporary.

sections.heading: Extension widens or narrows options
sections.text:
Extension can widen poor farmers’ options by teaching low-cost methods, sharing information, forming groups, linking farmers to credit and buyers, and involving women, youth and landless people. It can narrow options when advice is top-down, favours richer or male farmers, promotes costly inputs without finance, ignores local knowledge, or serves only one crop.

Example: an agent visits only farmers who can buy fertiliser. Amina, a smallholder, is left out, so her choices shrink. If the agent demonstrates compost, helps a savings group and links farmers to buyers, Amina can test a low-cost option and keep more of her harvest. Extension is not neutral: who is reached shapes whether livelihoods improve.

keyPoints: The sustainable livelihoods framework groups assets into human, natural, physical, financial and social capital.
Poverty is multidimensional, not just low income; national poverty lines vary by country and year.
Food security has four pillars: availability, access, utilisation and stability.
Extension can widen options through advice, groups, market links and inclusion.
Extension can narrow options through top-down advice, bias to richer or male farmers, and costly technologies without finance.
Ask who is reached and what is promoted, because extension is not neutral.

en.title: Agricultural Systems and Farm Production Basics
en.short: Main farming systems, their crop and livestock enterprises, and the agronomic and husbandry limits on advice.

sections.heading: Farming systems
sections.text:
A farming system is the set of crops, livestock and practices a household combines with its land, labour and capital. In Africa the main types are shifting cultivation, where land is rested to recover fertility; mixed crop-livestock smallholdings, the most common; pastoralism, herding on rangeland; and plantation or irrigated commercial systems. Elsewhere, specialised arable farms, ranches and intensive horticulture are common.

Rainfall, population density and market access decide which system fits a place. Advice that suits one zone can fail in another.

sections.heading: Enterprises within systems
sections.text:
Cereals (maize, sorghum, millet, rice), legumes (cowpea, groundnut, soybean), root and tuber crops (cassava, yam) and tree crops (cocoa, oil palm, coffee) are the main crop enterprises. Livestock includes cattle, sheep, goats, poultry and pigs.

In mixed systems, manure and draught power link crops and animals. Spreading enterprises also spreads risk and labour across the season.

sections.heading: Agronomic limits
sections.text:
Crop advice must respect growing-season length, rainfall amount and distribution, soil depth, texture, pH and fertility, and a variety’s maturity and pest tolerance. Sowing date, spacing, plant population, rotation and intercropping follow from these.

Example: a farmer in Kano harvests 2.5 t of maize per hectare; a trial with improved seed and fertiliser gives 4 t/ha. The yield gap is 4 − 2.5 = 1.5 t/ha, which is 1.5 ÷ 4 = 37.5% of the potential. Advice should attack the binding limit, such as late sowing or no fertiliser, not the seed alone.

sections.heading: Animal husbandry limits
sections.text:
Livestock advice depends on feed quantity and quality, water, breed adaptation to heat and disease, housing and veterinary control. Stocking rate, the number of animals per hectare, must match forage supply; overstocking degrades rangeland.

Trypanosomiasis, a disease spread by tsetse flies, limits cattle in infested areas, so tolerant breeds or control measures matter. Poultry need steady feed and vaccination.

keyPoints: A farming system is the mix of crops, livestock and practices a household uses on its land.
Mixed crop-livestock smallholdings are the most common system in Africa.
Crop advice must fit the growing season, soil and variety, not the other way round.
Yield gap = potential yield − actual yield, usually expressed as a share of potential.
Stocking rate must match forage supply or rangeland degrades.
Breed adaptation and disease pressure set limits on livestock advice.

en.title: Communication Basics for Extension
en.short: Communication defined, the source to feedback loop, one-way and two-way talk, noise and credibility.

sections.heading: The communication loop
sections.text:
Communication is the process of sharing information and ideas so that meaning is understood. In extension, an officer must not only speak; the farmer must understand.

The source starts the message and decides what to say. The message is the information, advice or idea sent, in words, pictures or a demonstration. The channel is the route used, such as radio, a phone call, a poster or a farm visit. The receiver is the person or group who interprets it. Feedback is the receiver’s response, which shows whether the meaning arrived. These parts form a loop, not a straight line.

sections.heading: One-way and two-way
sections.text:
One-way communication flows from source to receiver with little or no feedback. A radio broadcast or leaflet is an example. It reaches many people quickly and cheaply, but the source cannot tell what was misunderstood.

Two-way communication allows questions and answers, as in a farm visit or group discussion. It is slower and reaches fewer people, but it lets the source check understanding and adjust the message. Good extension often combines both: mass media for awareness, then face-to-face discussion for detail.

sections.heading: Noise and credibility
sections.text:
Noise is anything that interferes with the message and changes what is heard. It may be physical, such as radio static or market noise; language noise, such as technical words or dialect; or psychological, such as fear or distrust.

Credibility is the receiver’s judgement that the source is trustworthy and knows the subject. A message from a known, fair and skilled source is more likely to be accepted. If farmers doubt the source, they may hear the words but reject the advice.

sections.heading: A short case
sections.text:
Amina, an extension officer, first sends a radio message about maize spacing. Some farmers miss the detail because of poor signal, and others distrust the station.

Later she meets a farmer group in Kaduna, Nigeria, with a demonstration and asks questions. Feedback shows that seed supply is the real concern, so she changes her advice.

keyPoints: Communication is sharing meaning, not just sending information.
The source sends a message through a channel to a receiver, and feedback closes the loop.
One-way communication is fast and wide but hides misunderstanding.
Two-way communication is slower but allows checking and adjustment.
Noise is any interference that changes what the receiver hears.
Credibility is the receiver’s trust in the source, and low credibility can make farmers reject good advice.

en.title: Teaching and Learning in Extension
en.short: How adults learn, learning by doing, and choosing lecture, demonstration, discussion or problem-posing.

sections.heading: How adults learn
sections.text:
The best-known set of ideas about adult learning is andragogy, as distinct from pedagogy, the teaching of children. Malcolm Knowles argued that adults are self-directed, bring experience, want learning relevant to their work, and prefer problem-centred teaching. They are motivated by internal goals, such as a better harvest, more than by certificates. An agent who lectures farmers without asking about their experience may meet resistance.

Adults learn when they see a gap between what they know and what they need. Start from the farmer’s own problem, then introduce the new idea. Respect existing knowledge, and remember that learning is social: farmers learn from each other, not only from the agent.

sections.heading: Learning by doing
sections.text:
Learning by doing means people understand and remember better when they perform a task themselves. It rests on experiential learning, described by John Dewey and later David Kolb. Kolb’s cycle is: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, and active experimentation. The agent sets a real task, lets the farmer do it, then guides reflection on what happened and why.

For example, an agent in a rice village wants farmers to try a new spacing. She gives each farmer a marked rope and a small plot. They plant with the rope, compare it with their usual spacing, and discuss differences in tillering, the growth of side shoots, and yield. The skill is learned in the hand and eye, not only the ear.

sections.heading: Choosing a method
sections.text:
Lecture: one-way talk; efficient for awareness with many people, weak for skills.
Demonstration: the agent shows and farmers practise; best for a new skill with a small group.
Discussion: two-way exchange; good for attitudes and complex choices, using farmers’ experience.
Problem-posing: learners analyse their own problem and act; good for empowerment and local priorities.
Match the method to the message: facts to many, use a lecture; a skill, demonstrate; a decision, discuss; a community’s own problem, pose it.

keyPoints: Andragogy treats adults as self-directed, experienced and problem-centred learners.
Learning by doing follows Kolb’s cycle: experience, reflection, conceptualisation and experimentation.
Lecture suits facts to large audiences but is weak for building practical skills.
Demonstration suits a new skill with a small group because farmers practise and see results.
Discussion suits attitudes and complex decisions by drawing on farmers’ experience.
Problem-posing suits empowerment and locally defined problems, with learners as active analysts.

en.title: Mathematics and Statistics for Extension Work
en.short: Percentages, ratios, averages, index numbers, survey tables and charts, with farm yield and benefit-cost examples.

sections.heading: Percentages, ratios, averages
sections.text: A percentage is a part per hundred: percentage = (part ÷ whole) × 100. A ratio compares two quantities, usually in the same units. An average summarises a group, usually the mean: mean = sum of values ÷ number of values. For a farm, yield = total output ÷ area harvested. If a farmer harvests 4,800 kg of maize from 1.6 ha, yield = 4,800 ÷ 1.6 = 3,000 kg/ha. If revenue is 960,000 naira and cost is 640,000 naira, the benefit-cost ratio is 960,000 ÷ 640,000 = 1.5. A ratio below 1 means a loss.

sections.heading: Averages and index numbers
sections.text: The mean is sensitive to extreme values. The median, the middle ordered value, is safer for incomes or farm sizes. An index number compares a value with a base value: index = (current value ÷ base value) × 100. If base maize price is 40,000 naira per tonne and current price is 50,000 naira, index = (50,000 ÷ 40,000) × 100 = 125. This is 25 per cent above the base. Always state the base period and unit.

sections.heading: Surveys, tables and charts
sections.text: In a simple survey, code each response, tally the codes, then tabulate frequency and percentage. For 40 farmers, if 10 use improved seed, percentage = (10 ÷ 40) × 100 = 25 per cent. A table needs clear headings, units and a total. Check that percentages add to 100, allowing for rounding. Bar charts compare categories, line charts show change over time, and pie charts show parts of a whole. Read axis labels and scales; a cut axis can exaggerate a small change.

sections.heading: Worked check
sections.text: A farmer has 2 ha and harvests 5,000 kg. Mean yield = 5,000 ÷ 2 = 2,500 kg/ha. Revenue is 1,000,000 naira and cost is 800,000 naira. Benefit-cost ratio = 1,000,000 ÷ 800,000 = 1.25. Net benefit = 1,000,000 − 800,000 = 200,000 naira. Check: 800,000 × 1.25 = 1,000,000.

keyPoints: Percentage = (part ÷ whole) × 100.
Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values; the median is the middle ordered value.
Yield = total output ÷ area harvested; keep the units consistent (for example, kg and ha).
Benefit-cost ratio = total benefit ÷ total cost; below 1 means a loss.
Index number = (current value ÷ base value) × 100; state the base period.
In a survey table, give frequency and percentage, and check totals and chart scales.

en.title: Diffusion of Innovations and Adoption
en.short: Rogers’ diffusion model, adopter categories, the innovation-decision process, and adoption, rejection and discontinuance.

sections.heading: Rogers’ model
sections.text: Diffusion is the spread of an innovation, meaning an idea, practice or object seen as new, through communication channels over time among members of a social system. Rogers names four elements: the innovation, channels, time and the social system. Adoption is the decision to use it fully. The model is about communication and social influence, not just the technology’s quality.

sections.heading: Adopter categories
sections.text: Rogers groups adopters by innovativeness, the speed of first use. Innovators (about 2.5%) are venturesome; early adopters (13.5%) are respected local leaders; the early majority (34%) deliberate; the late majority (34%) are sceptical and adopt under pressure; laggards (16%) are traditional and isolated. These are analytical categories, not fixed labels. Opinion leaders in the early categories often speed diffusion.

sections.heading: Decision process
sections.text: The innovation-decision process has five stages: knowledge (learning what it is and how it works), persuasion (forming a favourable or unfavourable attitude), decision (adopt or reject), implementation (putting it into use), and confirmation (seeking reinforcement, which may reverse the decision). Perceived attributes shape speed: relative advantage, compatibility, low complexity, trialability and observability. Adoption is faster when farmers can test on a small plot, see results, and fit the practice to existing farming. It is slower with high cost, uncertain markets, weak extension contact, risk and social disapproval.

sections.heading: Adoption and rejection
sections.text: Rejection is a decision not to adopt. It can be passive (never seriously considered) or active (tried and refused). Discontinuance is later rejection after adoption, often because inputs fail, yields disappoint or the practice is too labour-demanding. In a case, suppose Amina in northern Nigeria tries a new maize variety on 0.2 ha. She adopts after a good trial, then discontinues when seed supply fails. That is discontinuance, not initial rejection.

keyPoints: Diffusion is the spread of an innovation through channels over time in a social system.
Rogers’ adopter categories are innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority and laggards.
The innovation-decision process runs knowledge, persuasion, decision, implementation, confirmation.
Adoption is faster when an innovation has clear relative advantage, fits local practice, is simple, trialable and observable.
Rejection is a decision not to adopt; discontinuance is rejection after adoption.
Opinion leaders, input supply, markets and risk shape adoption speed.

en.title: Extension Models and Approaches
en.short: Comparing training and visit, farmer field schools, farming systems, commodity and cost-sharing models.

sections.heading: Five models
sections.text: An extension model is an organised way of linking farmers with advice, learning and services. The training and visit (T&V) system, promoted by the World Bank in the 1970s and 1980s, used regular, often fortnightly visits by field staff to selected contact farmers, backed by scheduled in-service training. It fits simple, seasonal messages in a stable public service. It is weak for complex farm problems, can favour contact farmers, and is costly to sustain.

sections.heading: Learning and systems
sections.text: Farmer field schools (FFS) are season-long group learning processes based on observation and experiment in the field. They suit pest management, soil health and complex decisions where farmers must adapt. They need skilled facilitators and are costly per farmer. The farming systems approach treats the farm and household as one system. It diagnoses constraints across crops, livestock, labour and markets, then tests options on farms. It fits mixed farms and complex problems, but needs interdisciplinary staff, data and time.

sections.heading: Commodity and cost-sharing
sections.text: Commodity-based extension is organised around one product, such as cocoa, cotton or dairy, often by a board, company or cooperative. It gives specialised advice and market links, but may neglect other enterprises and favour commercial producers. Cost-sharing means beneficiaries pay part of the service cost through fees, levies or in-kind contributions. It can improve accountability and sustainability, but may exclude poor farmers and reduce use. It fits where farmers have cash income and services are demand-led.

sections.heading: Choosing a model
sections.text: No model is best everywhere. Use T&V for a clear national campaign, FFS for farmer-led learning, farming systems for mixed-farm diagnosis, commodity models for specialised value chains, and cost-sharing where services can be paid for. In a mixed maize and poultry district, a farming systems survey may identify feed cost as the main constraint; a commodity model could then organise feed buying, while FFS helps farmers test cheaper rations. Check current national policy, because models are often combined.

keyPoints: T&V uses regular visits and in-service training but is top-down and costly.
FFS builds farmer learning through season-long field observation and experiment.
The farming systems approach treats farm and household as one system and fits mixed farms.
Commodity-based extension gives specialised advice but can neglect other enterprises.
Cost-sharing can improve sustainability but may exclude poor farmers.
Models are often combined; choose by problem, farmers and funding.

en.title: Extension Methods and Media
en.short: Individual, group and mass methods, demonstrations, visits, field days, tours and media channels.

sections.heading: Three families of methods
sections.text: Extension methods are the ways advisers organise contact with farmers. They fall into three families. Individual methods reach one farmer or household at a time, so they suit diagnosis, confidential advice and trust building. Group methods bring several farmers together to see, discuss and practise, so they suit skill learning and shared problem solving. Mass methods send one message to many people, so they suit awareness, timely alerts and broad information. A medium is the carrier, such as print, radio or a phone. A method is the arrangement of people and learning.

sections.heading: Individual and group methods
sections.text: Farm and home visits are the classic individual method. The agent sees the farm, the home and the family context, and can give specific advice. They are costly in staff time, so use them for priority cases. Demonstrations are group methods. A method demonstration teaches a skill step by step, such as correct spacing or safe spraying. A result demonstration compares a new practice with the local one over a season, so farmers see the difference. Field days open a demonstration or trial site to many visitors. Tours take farmers to other farms, markets or research stations to widen experience.

sections.heading: Mass media and mobile
sections.text: Print includes leaflets, posters and newsletters. It suits reference and detail but needs literacy and distribution. Radio reaches distant listeners quickly and in local languages, and is strong for alerts and discussion programmes. Video shows processes that words describe poorly. Mobile phones add SMS, voice calls, WhatsApp groups and short videos. They allow reminders, questions and photos, but network coverage, cost, literacy and unequal access can limit use.

sections.heading: Matching method to purpose
sections.text: Match the method to the purpose. For a new spraying skill, use a group demonstration and follow up with visits. For a pest alert, use radio and SMS. For a complex farm plan, use a visit. In a case in northern Nigeria, an agent might announce a field day by radio and SMS, demonstrate a new rice spacing at the site, then visit two farmers who need help adapting it.

keyPoints: Individual methods suit specific advice and trust building but cost staff time.
Group methods suit skill learning and shared problem solving.
Mass methods suit awareness and timely alerts but give less feedback.
A method demonstration teaches a skill; a result demonstration shows a practice over a season.
Field days and tours let farmers see and discuss practices away from their own farms.
Print, radio, video and mobile channels work best when combined with follow-up.

en.title: Teaching Aids and Message Design
en.short: Choosing, preparing and testing charts, posters, flannel boards, models and slides for extension teaching.

sections.heading: Choosing the aid
sections.text: A teaching aid is any object or picture that helps learners see an idea. Select it after you know the audience, the single message and the setting. A poster suits a market notice; a flannel board suits a step-by-step talk to a small group; a model suits a machine or soil profile; slides suit a dark room with power. Choose the simplest aid that carries the message. Check cost, transport, durability and whether learners can see it.

sections.heading: Preparing the aid
sections.text: Prepare from the learner’s view. One aid should carry one main idea. Use large lettering, strong contrast and few words. For a chart, plan the title, drawing and caption before drawing. For a flannel board, back pictures with sandpaper or felt so they hold. For a model, show the important part, not every detail. For slides, use one idea per slide and readable type. Test the aid at the distance learners will sit; a poster clear at arm’s length may fail at five metres.

sections.heading: Layout and language
sections.text: Clear layout follows a reading path: title at top, then the main picture, then short captions. Leave white space. Use no more than two type styles. Write in the local language learners speak, with familiar units and names. Check translations with a local speaker, because a word may carry a different meaning. Pictures should show local crops, tools, clothing and roles, including women and men where relevant.

sections.heading: Testing the message
sections.text: Pretest before use. Show the aid to a few people like the audience. Ask what they see, what it means and what they would do. Note confusion, missing steps and words that offend. Revise, then test again. Case: Amina prepares a poster on safe pesticide use for farmers in Kano. In the pretest, farmers did not recognise the skull symbol as a warning about poison. She replaces it with a picture of a person wearing gloves and a mask, and adds a Hausa caption. The second test shows the message is understood.

keyPoints: Select the simplest aid that fits the audience, message and setting.
One aid should carry one main idea, with large lettering and strong contrast.
Plan layout as title, main picture, then short captions, with white space.
Write in the learners’ local language and check translations with a local speaker.
Pretest the aid with people like the audience and revise what confuses them.
Test visibility at the distance learners will actually sit.

en.title: Extension Programme Planning
en.short: The planning cycle, finding farmer needs, objectives, activities, budgets, schedules and review.

sections.heading: The planning cycle
sections.text: Programme planning is the process of deciding what an extension service will do, for whom, why, and with what resources. It usually follows a cycle. Situation analysis describes the area, people, farming systems and existing services. Problem identification separates felt needs, the problems farmers themselves state, from underlying causes, so the programme addresses causes, not only symptoms. Objectives state the change expected. Good objectives are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, often called SMART. Activities are the methods and events chosen to reach each objective. Budgeting costs each activity. Scheduling places activities in a calendar, respecting seasons and labour peaks. Review checks progress and lessons, and feeds the next cycle.

sections.heading: Finding needs
sections.text: Needs can be found from three main sources. Surveys use questionnaires with a sample of farmers; they give comparable data but need careful sampling. Meetings with farmers, groups and local leaders reveal felt needs and priorities, though loud voices may dominate. Secondary data are records already collected, such as census reports, ministry statistics, research reports and project documents. Use several sources and cross-check them. A need is not automatically a priority: compare how many people are affected, how serious it is, and whether extension can realistically help.

sections.heading: Worked case
sections.text: Suppose an extension officer in Kano State, Nigeria, plans a dry-season tomato training programme. A survey of 40 farmers finds 30 report fruit rot. Meetings confirm storage and spraying timing as concerns. The officer sets an objective: 30 farmers apply two recommended practices by the next harvest. Activities: two field demonstrations and one group meeting. Budget: venue 10,000 naira, materials 15,000, transport 5,000, total 30,000 naira. Schedule: demonstrations in weeks 1 and 3, meeting in week 2. Review after each event checks attendance; practice adoption is checked later, by the next harvest.

keyPoints: Planning follows a cycle: situation analysis, problem identification, objectives, activities, budget, schedule and review.
SMART objectives are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Surveys, meetings and secondary data should be cross-checked when assessing needs.
Priority setting compares how many people are affected, how serious the problem is and whether extension can help.
A budget adds the cost of each activity; the worked case totals 30,000 naira.
Review checks progress and lessons and feeds the next planning cycle.

en.title: Management and Administration of Extension Services
en.short: Management functions, structure, span of control, supervision, appraisal and staff time allocation.

sections.heading: What managers do
sections.text:
Management is getting work done through other people. Administration is the wider function of setting policy, rules and procedures within which managers work. A classic list of management functions, from Luther Gulick, is planning, organising, staffing, directing, coordinating, reporting and budgeting.

In an extension service, planning sets the season’s programme, organising divides staff and territory, staffing recruits and trains, and reporting and budgeting feed the next cycle.

sections.heading: Structure and span of control
sections.text:
Organisation structure shows who commands whom. Line officers give direct orders; staff officers, such as subject-matter specialists, advise without commanding. Unity of command means each officer answers to one supervisor only. Span of control is the number of subordinates one supervisor can supervise well; it depends on distance, task difficulty and experience.

Example: if each field officer needs one supervision day a month, a supervisor with 8 officers uses 8 of about 20 working days. With 20 officers, supervision alone fills the month.

sections.heading: Supervision and appraisal
sections.text:
Supervision is the day-to-day guiding, checking and supporting of subordinates; it should be supportive, not only policing. Staff appraisal is a regular, recorded judgement of an officer against agreed targets, such as visits made, groups formed or farmers trained, and against behaviour such as honesty and teamwork.

Good practice uses self-assessment, a written record, feedback and a development plan. Appraisal by impression alone is unfair and unreliable.

sections.heading: Allocating time and inputs
sections.text: Time is the scarcest input. Budget field days first, then subtract office, reporting and training time. Worked example: an officer has 20 working days a month. Office and reporting take 4, training and meetings 2, leaving 14 field days. At two visits a day that is 28 visits a month, or 308 a year over 11 field months, allowing one month for leave. If 300 farmers each need 4 visits, 1,200 visits are needed. 1,200 ÷ 308 = 3.9, so 4 field officers. Transport and materials are costed per visit the same way.

keyPoints: Management functions are planning, organising, staffing, directing, coordinating, reporting and budgeting.
Line officers command; staff officers advise.
Span of control is the number of subordinates one supervisor can supervise well.
Supervision should support staff, not only check them.
Appraisal compares recorded performance with agreed targets and ends in a development plan.
Visits per officer per year = field days per month × visits per day × field months; divide total visits needed by this to get staff numbers.

en.title: Monitoring and Evaluation of Extension Programmes
en.short: Monitoring versus evaluation, formative versus summative, indicators, targets and feedback.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
sections.text:
Monitoring is the routine, continuous collection of information on whether activities go to plan: farmers trained, demonstrations held, inputs delivered. The team does it during implementation, asking whether we are doing things right.

Evaluation is a periodic, systematic judgement of worth: did the programme meet its objectives, and did it matter? It uses monitoring data plus special studies, and asks whether we were doing the right things. Monitoring tracks inputs, activities and outputs; evaluation also looks at outcomes and impact.

sections.heading: Formative and summative
sections.text:
Formative evaluation happens during the programme to improve it. It tests the design, messages, training content and delivery, and findings go straight back to the team. Pre-testing a training manual with 20 farmers is formative.

Summative evaluation happens at or after the end to judge results and decide whether to continue, expand or stop. It reports to funders and policymakers. The same data can serve both.

sections.heading: Indicators, targets, sources
sections.text:
An indicator is a measurable sign that something has been done or has changed. Good ones are specific, measurable and time-bound: farmers trained, share of trained farmers who adopted a practice, yield per hectare.

A target is the level an indicator should reach by a stated date, for example 400 farmers trained by June.

A data source is where the figure comes from: attendance registers, farm records, farm visits, household surveys, group discussions. Name the source and method for each indicator so figures can be checked.

sections.heading: Feeding findings back
sections.text:
Findings feed back in a review meeting that compares actual with target, asks why, and changes the design.

Case: a programme targets 400 farmers trained. Registers show 340 attended, 340 ÷ 400 = 85% of target. A follow-up survey finds 120 of the 340 trained, 120 ÷ 340 = 35.3%, adopted the practice, against a target of 50%. Most non-adopters were women who missed the field day, so the next phase adds a women’s field day and follow-up visits, with the same indicators.

keyPoints: Monitoring is continuous and internal; evaluation is periodic and judges worth.
Formative evaluation improves a running programme; summative evaluation judges results at or after the end.
An indicator is a measurable sign of change; a target is the level it should reach by a stated date.
Every indicator needs a named data source and method so the figure can be checked.
Findings feed back through a review meeting that compares actual with target and changes the design.
Keep the same indicators across rounds so results can be compared.

en.title: Participatory Rural Appraisal and Farmer Participation
en.short: Arnstein’s ladder, the shift from for to with farmers, and PRA/PLA tools such as maps and calendars.

sections.heading: Ladder of participation
sections.text: Arnstein’s ladder (1969) ranks participation by how much power people have. Its eight rungs are manipulation, therapy, informing, consultation, placation, partnership, delegated power and citizen control. The first two are non-participation; informing, consultation and placation are tokenism; partnership, delegated power and citizen control give real power. In extension, a meeting where farmers are only told a plan sits low. Partnership means farmers help set priorities, design activities and share decisions.

sections.heading: From for to with
sections.text: The shift from extension for farmers to extension with farmers changes who diagnoses problems and chooses solutions. In the older top-down model, extension staff decide and transfer technology to farmers. In participatory extension, farmers and staff analyse the farm and community together, use local knowledge, and agree on action. Participation is a scale, not a single event; Arnstein’s ladder helps check whether it is genuine or token.

sections.heading: PRA and PLA tools
sections.text: PRA (Participatory Rural Appraisal) is a family of methods that helps rural people map, analyse and plan their own situation. PLA (Participatory Learning and Action) is a broader term for similar learning and action processes. Common tools include resource mapping, where people draw local land, water, crops and infrastructure; transect walks, where staff and farmers walk a line across the area and note differences; ranking, where people order preferences, problems or wealth; and seasonal calendars, which show rainfall, labour, food, income and pests across the year.

sections.heading: Illustrative case
sections.text: Suppose Amina, an extension officer in northern Nigeria, visits a village. Instead of a fixed plan, she walks a transect with Musa and other farmers. They draw a resource map, rank three main constraints, and make a seasonal calendar. They see that water shortage is worst in the dry season and labour peaks at weeding. They agree to test a small water-harvesting plot and review it together. Amina’s role is facilitator, not lecturer.

keyPoints: Arnstein’s ladder ranks participation by how much power people have, from manipulation to citizen control.
Informing and consultation are tokenism; partnership and citizen control share real power.
Participatory extension moves from deciding for farmers to analysing and acting with them.
PRA and PLA use visual group tools so people can analyse their own situation.
Resource maps show local resources, transect walks reveal variation, ranking sets priorities, and seasonal calendars show change over the year.
Participation can be tokenistic, so ask who decides and who benefits.

en.title: Farmer Field Schools and Experiential Learning
en.short: The FFS season, field plot, weekly learning cycle, IPM content and adaptation to new subjects.

sections.heading: The FFS season
sections.text:
A Farmer Field School (FFS) is a group of farmers who meet through a whole crop or production season on a field, learning by observing, testing and deciding together. The season usually starts near planting and ends at harvest. A facilitator guides the group but does not lecture. This is experiential learning: learning by doing and reflecting on results.

The field school plot is a real field that the group manages, not a show plot kept perfect by staff. Farmers see the results of their own decisions, including mistakes, and review the season at the end.

sections.heading: Plot and weekly cycle
sections.text:
Each week the group meets at the plot. In small groups, farmers observe sample plants and record pests, diseases, weeds, natural enemies, soil and weather. They draw a simple field map or plant diagram. This is agro-ecosystem analysis (AESA): a structured look at the field as a living system.

The group then discusses what it found, decides what to do, and carries out the task. The cycle is observe, record, discuss, decide, act. For example, at one meeting Amina’s group finds aphids on maize; they count them, note ladybirds, and decide to keep monitoring and let the ladybirds work before any spray. Over the season these steps build confidence and problem-solving skills.

sections.heading: IPM and adaptation
sections.text:
Integrated pest management (IPM) was the classic FFS content. It combines monitoring, cultural methods, biological control and careful use of pesticides only when needed. Farmers learn to identify pests and natural enemies, study life cycles, and judge whether action is justified. The model is often traced to rice IPM work in Indonesia with support from FAO, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.

The same season-long, field-based method has been adapted to soil fertility, water, livestock, nutrition and health. Adaptation needs a local curriculum and trained facilitators; changing the topic alone is not enough.

keyPoints: An FFS is a season-long, field-based group learning process, not a one-day lecture.
The field school plot is a real managed field where farmers learn from their own decisions.
The weekly cycle is observe, record, discuss, decide and act, often using agro-ecosystem analysis.
IPM was the classic FFS content: monitor pests and natural enemies and use pesticides only when justified.
FFS has been adapted to many subjects, but each adaptation needs a local curriculum and trained facilitators.
Experiential learning works because farmers test ideas in their own fields and review results together.

en.title: Linking Extension with Research and Input Supply
en.short: How research, extension, farmers and input suppliers exchange information through trials and feedback.

sections.heading: The linkage system
sections.text: A linkage is a planned working relationship between research, extension, farmers and input suppliers. Research generates and tests knowledge. Extension helps farmers understand options and sends problems back. Farmers test, adapt, accept or reject. Input suppliers provide seed, fertiliser, crop protection products and equipment. Information must flow both ways. Recommendations, trial results and safety advice move towards farmers. Observations on performance, cost, risk and demand move back. A one-way pipeline from scientists to farmers is weak because it ignores local conditions and input availability.

sections.heading: On-farm trials
sections.text: On-farm trials are experiments in farmers’ fields under real soil, weather, labour and management conditions. They may be researcher-managed or farmer-managed. Their purpose is adaptive research: checking whether a technology that worked on a research station also works locally. Technology verification is a formal step before wide recommendation. It compares the new practice with the farmer’s current practice using yield, cost, labour, risk and farmer preference, not yield alone. Repeat verification across seasons and sites because one season proves little.

sections.heading: Input supply
sections.text: Input supply is part of the linkage. A technology cannot be adopted if farmers cannot obtain the seed, fertiliser or credit it requires, or if the input is fake or too costly. Extension workers need current information on products, correct use, safety and local dealers. Dealers need demand forecasts and clear labelling. Input quality is regulated in many countries, so advisers should check the current official list.

sections.heading: Feedback to researchers
sections.text: Feedback must be organised, not anecdotal. Useful methods include field days, farmer panels, short records of yield and cost, and trial reports. Suppose Amina, a researcher, recommends a new maize variety near Kano, Nigeria. Musa, an extension agent, arranges trials on ten farms. Farmers report that the variety yields well but needs more fertiliser than they can afford. That feedback can lead researchers to test lower-input management or breeders to select for low-fertility tolerance. Without feedback, the recommendation may fail.

keyPoints: Linkage is a planned, two-way relationship among research, extension, farmers and input suppliers.
On-farm trials test a technology under real farm conditions and are a form of adaptive research.
Technology verification compares a new practice with the farmer’s current practice before wide recommendation.
Input supply belongs in the linkage because unavailability, high cost or fake inputs block adoption.
Structured farmer feedback tells researchers about performance, cost, risk and acceptability.
Repeat trials across seasons and sites because one season proves little.

en.title: Technology Generation, Transfer and Adaptation
en.short: Generation, transfer, adaptation and use of farm technology, recommendation domains and farmer innovation.

sections.heading: Four stages
sections.text: Technology generation is the creation and testing of a new practice, variety or tool, usually by researchers on an experiment station. Transfer is the movement of that technology and its knowledge to farmers through extension, media, input dealers or lead farmers. Adaptation is the local adjustment of the technology, for example to soil, rainfall, labour, equipment or market. Use is the farmer’s decision to apply it in the farm system. The stages overlap: farmers adapt while using, and their feedback should shape generation.

sections.heading: Recommendation domains
sections.text: A recommendation domain is a group of farms with similar climate, soil, rainfall, cropping system, labour and market conditions, for which one recommendation is likely to work. It is not a single farm and not a whole region. Advisers define domains using agro-ecological and socio-economic data. A technology can be transferred within a domain, but it needs testing before crossing into another domain.

sections.heading: Station versus farm
sections.text: A technology that works at a research station may fail on farms because stations control conditions. Plots are uniform, inputs arrive on time, irrigation is available, labour is skilled and pests are few. Farms are variable and risk-prone. Soils differ, rain is uncertain, cash and labour are short, and farmers must weigh risk, taste, storage and market price, not yield alone. A high-yielding variety that needs fertiliser may fail where fertiliser is costly or late. A mechanised tool may fail on small, scattered plots.

sections.heading: Farmer innovation
sections.text: Farmers are not passive receivers. Farmer innovation is the testing and adaptation farmers do themselves, such as selecting seed, modifying tools or building water-harvesting structures. Participatory on-farm trials and farmer field days bring researchers, advisers and farmers together. Case: a maize variety tested on a station in Nigeria with fertiliser and timely rain may yield well. In a village near Kaduna, late rain and no fertiliser can make it perform poorly, while a local early variety is safer. Advisers should test across recommendation domains and treat farmer feedback as evidence.

keyPoints: Generation creates a technology; transfer moves it; adaptation fits it; use applies it.
Recommendation domains group farms with similar conditions for which one recommendation is likely to work.
Research station success does not guarantee farm success because stations control conditions that farms cannot.
Farmers adapt and innovate, so their feedback should shape technology development.
Test a technology on farms across recommendation domains before scaling it.

en.title: Gender, Youth and Social Inclusion in Extension
en.short: Gender roles, gender analysis, practical and strategic interests, access gaps and inclusive design.

sections.heading: Gender roles and analysis
sections.text: Sex refers to biological differences; gender refers to the social roles and expectations that a society assigns to women and men. Gender roles in farming are learned and change over time: who clears land, plants, weeds, sells produce or manages money differs by crop, region and household. Gender analysis is the systematic study of these differences, including who does what, who owns or controls land, credit, inputs and information, and who decides. Age, marital status and income also shape opportunities.

sections.heading: Practical and strategic interests
sections.text: Practical gender interests concern immediate living conditions: water, fuel, food, cash and safer farming. Strategic gender interests concern lasting change in unequal power relations, such as secure land rights, voice in cooperatives or freedom from violence. The two can overlap. A women’s vegetable group may meet a practical need for income while also building confidence to speak at meetings, which is strategic. Extension workers should not assume that all women, or all youth, have the same interests.

sections.heading: Access and control
sections.text: Access to land, credit, inputs and extension contact is often unequal. Land may be held under customary tenure, inheritance rules or formal title, and women and young people may farm land they do not control. Credit often requires collateral or a formal account. Inputs may be sold through networks men dominate. Extension contact may be lower where visits are timed for male-headed plots, held far away, or led only by male agents. These are common patterns, not universal; local diagnosis is needed.

sections.heading: Designing inclusive services
sections.text: Design services with women and youth. Collect sex- and age-disaggregated data. Use female agents, and hold sessions at accessible times and places. Case: Amina’s vegetable plots were ignored because demonstrations followed male maize fields; a female agent ran evening vegetable sessions and linked her group to savings and an input dealer. Link groups to credit, markets and leadership. Youth may need start-up finance, land access, digital advisory and market linkages. Youth age definitions vary by country; check current policy.

keyPoints: Gender is socially learned; sex is biological.
Gender analysis examines roles, resources, power and needs by sex, age and context.
Practical interests meet immediate needs; strategic interests challenge unequal power relations.
Women and youth often face weaker access to land, credit, inputs and extension contact, but this varies locally.
Inclusive design uses sex- and age-disaggregated data, female agents, accessible timing and group linkages.
Youth definitions vary by country, so check the current official policy.

en.title: Farmer Groups, Cooperatives and Federations
en.short: Types, functions, cooperative principles, formation, leadership, records and common group problems.

sections.heading: Types and principles
sections.text:
Farmer organisations range from informal groups to cooperatives and federations. A farmer group is a small set of farmers who meet for a shared purpose, for example buying inputs or selling together. A cooperative is a member-owned, democratically controlled business that serves its members. A federation is a secondary body whose members are primary cooperatives; it can buy in bulk, market produce, lobby and train.

The International Cooperative Alliance states seven principles: voluntary and open membership; democratic member control; member economic participation; autonomy and independence; education, training and information; cooperation among cooperatives; and concern for community. One member has one vote, not one vote per share. Surplus may be shared by member patronage or kept as reserves. Registration rules differ by country, so check the cooperative law and registrar.

sections.heading: Formation and leadership
sections.text:
Formation starts with a felt need and a clear purpose. Members agree on eligibility, shares or fees, duties, meeting times, rules and a simple constitution. They register with the proper authority for legal status. Leaders are elected, serve fixed terms and report to the general meeting. Good leaders listen, delegate, keep promises and manage conflict early. Include women and young farmers in decisions, not only in attendance.

Case: a village maize group of 30 farmers agrees to buy fertiliser together. Each member pays a deposit, the treasurer records it, and the secretary keeps minutes. They elect a five-person committee and review prices at a general meeting before ordering.

sections.heading: Records and problems
sections.text:
Records are the group’s memory. Keep a membership register, minutes, a cash book, receipts, a stock book, loan records and an asset list. Simple, honest records let members check money and decide. A yearly audit builds trust.

Common problems include free riding (taking benefits without contributing), elite capture by leaders, poor attendance, weak records, unpaid dues, conflict and dependence on outside aid. Prevent them with clear rules, open accounts, rotation of leaders, regular meetings and fair conflict procedures.

keyPoints: Farmer groups can be informal, cooperatives are member-owned businesses, and federations are owned by primary cooperatives.
Cooperatives follow seven International Cooperative Alliance principles, including one member one vote and concern for community.
Formation needs a clear purpose, agreed rules, registration where required and elected accountable leaders.
Records such as minutes, cash books and membership registers protect members and support decisions.
Common problems include free riding, elite capture, weak records and conflict; clear rules and open accounts reduce them.
Registration and cooperative law differ by country, so check the current official rules.

en.title: Agribusiness, Value Chains and Market Linkages
en.short: Mapping value chains, market information, contract farming, aggregation and links to buyers and finance.

sections.heading: Mapping the chain
sections.text:
An agricultural value chain is the sequence of activities and actors that move a product from input supply to the consumer: input suppliers, producers, aggregators or traders, processors, wholesalers, retailers, consumers. Support services include extension, transport, finance and standards. Mapping shows product, money and information flows and who performs each function.

Value added is the increase in worth from cleaning, grading, storage, processing or packaging. It is not profit: a stage may add value yet earn a thin margin. Risk sits unevenly. Farmers carry production, weather, pest and price risk; traders carry storage and payment risk; processors carry quality and market risk.

sections.heading: Information, contracts, aggregation
sections.text:
Market information services share prices, volumes and buyer requirements by radio, SMS or apps. They help when timely, local and reliable; stale prices mislead. They cut search costs and aid bargaining.

Contract farming is an agreement between a farmer and a buyer or processor setting quantity, quality, price, inputs, credit and payment. It can reduce risk and open finance, but watch side-selling (selling outside the contract to another buyer), unfair terms, quality rejection and dependence on one buyer.

Aggregation is collecting smallholders’ output to reach the volume and quality a buyer needs, through cooperatives or traders. It lowers transaction costs and improves bargaining, but needs trust and records.

sections.heading: Extension links, example
sections.text:
Extension links farmers to buyers and finance by sharing market information, teaching quality and records, helping groups aggregate, and referring farmers to lenders. It should inform and organise, not give legal or financial advice beyond its competence.

Case: a farmer sells 100 kg of graded maize at 200 per kg, earning 20,000. An aggregator buys at 200 (20,000) and sells at 260 (26,000); after other costs of 3,000, the net margin is 3,000. A retailer buys at 260 (26,000) and sells at 320 (32,000); after costs of 4,000, the net margin is 2,000. The farmer’s share of the final 32,000 is 20,000 ÷ 32,000 = 62.5 per cent.

keyPoints: A value chain runs from input supply to the consumer, with support services alongside.
Value added is not the same as profit.
Risk is unevenly shared: farmers carry production and price risk, traders storage and payment risk.
Market information helps only when timely, local and reliable.
Contract farming can reduce risk and open finance but creates dependence and side-selling risk.
Aggregation lowers transaction costs and improves bargaining when groups keep good records.

en.title: Farm Planning and Budgeting for Advisers
en.short: Enterprise budgets, gross margins, partial budgets and break-even analysis for farm advice.

sections.heading: Planning and budgets
sections.text: Farm planning helps a farmer choose what to produce, how much, and with which resources. An enterprise budget lists expected returns and costs for one enterprise, such as one hectare of maize, for a season. It separates variable costs, which change with output, from fixed costs, which do not. Gross margin is gross revenue minus variable costs. It compares enterprises when fixed costs are shared and hard to allocate. Use local, current prices and yields, and state that the figures are estimates. An adviser should write down the assumptions so the farmer can check them.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Suppose one hectare. Maize: yield 2,000 kg at 250 per kg gives revenue 500,000. Variable costs: seed 20,000, fertiliser 80,000, labour 100,000, other 30,000, total 230,000. Gross margin = 500,000 − 230,000 = 270,000. Groundnut: yield 1,200 kg at 500 per kg gives 600,000. Variable costs: seed 60,000, fertiliser 40,000, labour 120,000, other 30,000, total 250,000. Gross margin = 600,000 − 250,000 = 350,000. Groundnut is better by 80,000 per hectare if land is the limiting resource (the input in shortest supply) and the estimates hold. Check: 350,000 − 270,000 = 80,000.

sections.heading: Partial and break-even
sections.text: A partial budget assesses a small change, not the whole farm. Net change = added returns + reduced costs − added costs − reduced returns. Adopt the change if the net change is positive. Break-even analysis finds the output or price at which revenue equals total cost. Break-even quantity = fixed costs ÷ (price per unit − variable cost per unit). Break-even price = total cost ÷ expected output. These tools help an adviser compare options, but they do not replace checking risk, labour, land and market limits. Use current market prices and local cost data.

keyPoints: An enterprise budget lists returns and costs for one enterprise over a season.
Gross margin = gross revenue − variable costs; it ignores fixed costs.
Compare enterprises by gross margin per unit of the limiting resource, not only per hectare.
Partial budget net change = added returns + reduced costs − added costs − reduced returns.
Break-even quantity = fixed costs ÷ (price per unit − variable cost per unit).
Break-even price = total cost ÷ expected output; use current local prices and check assumptions.

en.title: Farm Records, Accounts and Analysis
en.short: Farm record types, cash and accrual accounts, profit, cost of production and returns to labour.

sections.heading: Record types
sections.text: Farm records are organised facts about the farm. Production records note area, yields, livestock births, deaths and weights. Financial records include receipts, invoices, cash book and bank statements. Resource and inventory records list land, tools, stock and feed. Labour records show who worked, days and wages. Good records are complete, timely and simple enough to keep.

sections.heading: Cash and accrual
sections.text: A cash account records money received and paid. Cash surplus = cash in − cash out. It is useful for liquidity but not true profit, because it ignores unpaid bills, stock changes and depreciation. An accrual account records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred. Profit = total revenue − total expenses, including depreciation and changes in inventory. Depreciation is the yearly fall in value of durable assets such as tools.

sections.heading: Worked analysis
sections.text: Example: 2 ha maize yields 4,000 kg sold at 250 per kg, revenue 1,000,000. Costs: seed 40,000, fertiliser 120,000, hired labour 150,000, other 30,000, depreciation 60,000, rent 40,000; total 440,000. Profit = 1,000,000 − 440,000 = 560,000. Cost of production = 440,000 ÷ 4,000 = 110 per kg. Labour used 500 person-days. Returns to labour = (revenue − non-labour costs) ÷ labour days = (1,000,000 − 290,000) ÷ 500 = 1,420 per person-day.

sections.heading: Using the results
sections.text: Use the figures in advice. If market price is near or below 110 per kg, the farmer risks loss and should cut costs or raise yield. If returns to labour are below the local wage, labour is better used elsewhere or the system must change. Compare across seasons and enterprises, and check records before advising. Figures such as prices and wages change, so use current local data.

keyPoints: Farm records cover production, finance, resources, inventory and labour.
Cash surplus = cash in − cash out; it is not profit.
Accrual profit = total revenue − total expenses, including unpaid bills, stock changes and depreciation.
Cost of production per unit = total cost ÷ output.
Returns to labour = (revenue − non-labour costs) ÷ labour days.
Use cost per unit and returns to labour to advise on price, costs and labour use.

en.title: Economics and Financing of Extension Services
en.short: What extension costs, who pays, cost-sharing and fees, and cost-effectiveness and benefit-cost analysis.

sections.heading: What extension costs
sections.text:
Extension costs divide into fixed costs, which do not change with the number of farmers served (offices, vehicles, permanent staff), and variable costs, which rise with activity (fuel, printing, field day allowances). Staff pay and travel usually take the largest share of a public service budget.

Planners also separate recurrent costs (salaries, fuel, maintenance) from capital costs (buildings, vehicles, equipment). Donors often fund capital and leave recurrent costs to the state. If the state cannot pay them, the service can collapse when the project ends.

sections.heading: Who pays
sections.text:
Advice has features of a public good: one farmer’s use does not reduce another’s, and non-payers are hard to exclude. Private firms therefore under-supply it, which is the market-failure argument for public funding. Governments fund national services; donors fund time-limited projects; private firms such as input dealers, processors and contract-farming schemes advise the farmers they trade with; NGOs fund through projects.

Cost-sharing means farmers or farmer organisations pay part of the cost, in cash, labour or produce. Fee-based advice charges the user directly. Fees can improve accountability, but may exclude smallholders, women and remote farmers, so some systems use vouchers or free advice for these groups.

sections.heading: Cost-effectiveness
sections.text: Cost-effectiveness compares the cost of reaching a given result. Common ratios are cost per farmer reached, cost per farmer adopting a practice, and cost per unit of yield or income gained. Mass media are cheap per person reached but weak at changing practice; face-to-face methods cost more per person but often change practice more. Compare methods on the same outcome over the same period.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
All figures are in local currency. Four field agents at 900,000 each = 3,600,000. Fuel and travel 600,000. Office and materials 300,000. Total = 4,500,000 a year. The programme reaches 1,500 farmers.
Cost per farmer reached = 4,500,000 ÷ 1,500 = 3,000.
Suppose 500 farmers adopt, each gaining 12,000 a year. Benefit = 500 × 12,000 = 6,000,000.
