Benefit-cost ratio = 6,000,000 ÷ 4,500,000 = 1.33. Benefits exceed costs.

For gains spread over years, discount: NPV = Σ Bt ÷ (1 + r)^t − Σ Ct ÷ (1 + r)^t. A ratio above 1 is not proof of impact, because adopters may have adopted anyway.

keyPoints: Fixed costs do not vary with farmers served; variable costs do.
Recurrent costs (salaries, fuel) are the ones that decide whether a service survives.
Public funding is justified where advice is a public good and private firms under-supply it.
Cost-sharing and fees recover part of the cost but can exclude poorer farmers.
Cost per farmer reached = total cost ÷ number of farmers reached.
Benefit-cost ratio = total benefits ÷ total costs; over several years, discount both with NPV = Σ Bt ÷ (1 + r)^t − Σ Ct ÷ (1 + r)^t.

en.title: Information and Communication Technology in Extension
en.short: Mobile, radio, video, call centres, apps and digital advisory platforms, and choosing channels fairly.

sections.heading: Channels and uses
sections.text: Information and communication technology (ICT) in extension means electronic tools and services used to share advice, collect feedback and support decisions. Mobile phones are the most widespread channel: SMS for short alerts, voice calls for discussion and menu codes for simple queries on basic handsets. Community radio reaches wide audiences cheaply through programmes, jingles and phone-in sessions. Video and clips show practical skills such as pruning or safe spraying. Call centres let farmers speak to an adviser, while farm management apps help with records, budgets and reminders. Digital advisory platforms combine weather, market and crop information in a service.

sections.heading: Choosing a channel
sections.text: Choose a channel by asking who the audience is, what the message must achieve, how urgent it is, and what people can use. A warning needs speed and reach; a complex skill needs demonstration and discussion. Use several channels together, because repetition helps and each channel covers another’s weakness. In a maize district, an extension service wants farmers to scout for fall armyworm. A radio jingle in the local language reaches many people quickly. An SMS to registered farmers gives one clear action. A call centre answers questions. A video at a group meeting shows the insect and damage. This mix serves different listeners without assuming everyone has a smartphone.

sections.heading: Access, language and trust
sections.text: Access is uneven. A farmer may lack a charged phone, network coverage, airtime, electricity or the literacy to read SMS. Women, older people, disabled people and remote households are often left out. Radio and group video can include people with basic handsets, but radio is one-way and call centres have limited hours. Language matters: use local languages, clear speech and voice menus where reading is hard. Trust matters too. Advice is more accepted when it comes from a known extension agent, a respected farmer or a station with local credibility. Platforms must protect privacy, explain who owns the data and correct errors. Test a channel with the audience before scaling it.

keyPoints: ICT in extension includes mobile phones, radio, video, call centres, farm management apps and digital advisory platforms.
Choose channels by audience, purpose, urgency, literacy, language, cost and trust.
Use a mix of channels; each has strengths and limits.
Access is uneven because of devices, network, electricity, cost, literacy, gender, age and disability.
Local language, voice options and known local sources improve understanding and trust.
Test a channel with the audience and protect privacy before scaling it up.

en.title: Climate-Smart Agriculture and Advisory Services
en.short: CSA’s three goals, weather services, drought and flood response, soil and water conservation and advisory choices under risk.

sections.heading: What CSA means
sections.text:
Climate-smart agriculture (CSA) is an approach that aims to make farming more productive and resilient while reducing greenhouse gas emissions where possible. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) describes three goals: sustainably increase productivity and incomes; adapt and build resilience to climate change; and reduce or remove emissions where possible.

A practice that raises yields may also raise emissions, and a mitigation practice may cost labour. CSA is site-specific, so advisers assess trade-offs with farmers.

sections.heading: Weather and climate services
sections.text:
Weather and climate information services give farmers forecasts, early warnings and agrometeorological advisories, meaning weather-based farming advice. Seasonal forecasts help with crop and variety choice; short-term forecasts help with planting, spraying and harvesting. Advisers should explain that forecasts are probabilistic, not certain, and should state the uncertainty.

Radio, SMS and local-language messages can reach many farmers, but messages must be timely and linked to a clear action. A forecast without an option is not an advisory.

sections.heading: Drought, flood and conservation
sections.text:
Drought response includes early-maturing and drought-tolerant varieties, water harvesting, mulching, and contingency plans for livestock. Flood response includes raised beds, drainage, flood-tolerant crops, and moving seed and stores to higher ground. Soil and water conservation protects the resource base: contour bunds, terraces, grass strips, cover crops, conservation tillage and organic matter. These practices reduce runoff and evaporation and improve infiltration.

Advisers should match practices to slope, soil, rainfall and labour, because a technique that works on one farm may fail on another.

sections.heading: Advisory choices under risk
sections.text: Under risk, advisers help farmers compare options by expected return, stability and risk attitude. They use participatory discussion and demonstration plots. A small case: Amina grows sorghum in a dry area. The seasonal forecast predicts below-average rain. Her adviser does not simply say 'plant early'. They discuss early-maturing sorghum, tied ridges and mulching, and agree a trigger: if the rains fail by a set date, she switches to a shorter-season variety and keeps seed for replanting. This is a flexible plan, not a fixed instruction.

keyPoints: CSA has three goals: productivity, adaptation and mitigation, and they can conflict.
Weather advisories should pair probabilistic forecasts with clear, timely actions.
Drought and flood planning uses early warning, tolerant varieties and water management.
Soil and water conservation reduces runoff, evaporation and soil loss.
Under risk, advisers compare options with farmers and build flexible trigger-based plans.
Check for maladaptation: a practice should not raise emissions or vulnerability elsewhere.

en.title: Research Methods for Extension Studies
en.short: Design, sampling, questionnaires, interviews, coding, statistics, reliability, validity, bias and survey write-up.

sections.heading: Design and sampling
sections.text: Research design is the plan that links your question to the data you will collect. For an extension survey, state the purpose, the population (all farmers in the area), the sample (those you actually study) and the sampling frame (the list you draw from). Probability sampling, such as simple random sampling, gives every listed unit a known chance of selection and supports generalisation. Non-probability sampling, such as purposive sampling, is useful for quick or specialised work but limits generalisation. Record how you selected the sample and how many agreed.

sections.heading: Questions and interviews
sections.text: Write questionnaire items in short, neutral language. Closed questions give fixed answers and are easy to code; open questions allow explanation but need more analysis. Avoid leading questions, double questions and unexplained terms. Pilot the questionnaire on a few farmers and revise it. In an interview, use a guide, listen, probe gently and record answers consistently. Train interviewers so they ask questions in the same way.

sections.heading: Coding and statistics
sections.text: Code data by giving each response a number, for example yes = 1 and no = 0, and keep a codebook. Descriptive statistics summarise the sample: frequencies, percentages and means. Percentage = count ÷ total × 100. Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values. Example: 40 farmers are sampled and 24 use improved seed. Percentage = 24 ÷ 40 × 100 = 60%. If five yields are 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 tonnes, mean = (2+3+4+5+6) ÷ 5 = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 tonnes.

sections.heading: Quality and write-up
sections.text: Reliability is consistency: the same method should give similar results on repeat. Validity is whether the question measures what it claims. Common biases include selection bias, recall bias, interviewer bias and social desirability bias, where people give answers they think are expected. In a short report, describe purpose, methods, sample, findings and limitations, then give conclusions. Use tables and simple sentences. Do not claim more than the sample supports.

keyPoints: Research design links the survey question to the population, sample and data collection plan.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; non-probability sampling limits it.
Pilot questionnaires and train interviewers to reduce bias.
Code responses with a codebook before computing frequencies, percentages and means.
Percentage = count ÷ total × 100; mean = sum of values ÷ number of values.
Reliability is consistency, validity is measuring the intended concept, and limitations must be reported honestly.

en.title: Professional Ethics and Conduct in Extension
en.short: Duties to farmers, employers and the public, and managing conflicts when selling inputs and advising.

sections.heading: Duties to farmers
sections.text: Extension advice affects a farmer’s income and family. Be honest in claims: do not promise a yield, profit or cure you cannot support. Say what evidence shows and what is uncertain. Respect farmers: listen, avoid pressure, and value local knowledge. Keep private information confidential, including farm records, debts and family matters, unless the farmer consents or the law requires disclosure. Be impartial: base advice on the farmer’s needs, not on gender, ethnicity, religion, wealth or personal gain.

sections.heading: Employer and public
sections.text: To your employer, follow lawful instructions, keep honest records, use funds and vehicles for their purpose, and do not use your position for private business. To the public, protect health and the environment. Do not recommend unregistered pesticides or unsafe storage. Explain risks plainly. Codes of conduct differ by country and organisation, so read the code that governs your post.

sections.heading: Conflicts of interest
sections.text: A conflict of interest is when a personal interest could improperly influence your professional judgement. Selling inputs while giving advice is a common example. If you earn commission on a product, your advice may favour it. Manage the conflict: disclose it, compare equivalent alternatives, separate sales from advice where possible, and decline to advise where you benefit. Never use confidential farmer information to target sales.

sections.heading: Case in practice
sections.text: Amina is an extension agent in northern Nigeria who also sells fertiliser. A farmer, Musa, asks which fertiliser to use. Amina earns commission on Brand X. She should say she sells Brand X and earns commission, then compare Brand X with other products on nutrient content and price per bag. She should give Musa the figures and let him decide. If she cannot be impartial, she should refer him to another adviser. She must not tell other farmers about Musa’s debts.

keyPoints: Be honest about what advice can and cannot achieve.
Keep farmers’ private information confidential unless consent or law allows disclosure.
Give advice impartially, free of bias about gender, ethnicity, religion or wealth.
A conflict of interest is a personal interest that could improperly influence professional judgement.
Disclose commissions and separate selling inputs from giving advice where possible.
Codes of conduct vary by country and employer, so read the one that governs your work.

en.title: Extension Project, Field Attachment and Report Writing
en.short: Planning an extension project, doing field attachment, and writing a referenced report.

sections.heading: Finding a problem
sections.text:
Start with a problem that matters to farmers or an extension service, not a preferred method. Find it through field observation, records, discussions with farmers and staff, or a gap in knowledge. Write a problem statement: what is wrong, who is affected, where, and why it matters. Narrow it to fit your time.

For example, Amina, on attachment in a Nigerian extension office, hears farmers ask when to apply fertiliser after rain, but records show no local guide. Her statement describes this uncertainty without overclaiming.

sections.heading: Objectives and review
sections.text:
Objectives flow from the problem. A general objective states the aim; specific objectives are measurable tasks. Use verbs such as describe, compare, estimate or identify. Avoid prove or solve unless your design supports them.

The literature review shows what other studies found, where they disagree and what remains unclear. Use credible sources, report them accurately and avoid copying. Link each source to your objectives. End with a short gap statement that leads to your study.

sections.heading: Methods and data
sections.text:
Methodology explains how you will answer each objective. Describe the study area, population, sample and sampling method, instruments, data collection and analysis. If you use a questionnaire, say how you checked it.

For Amina, a questionnaire to 60 farmers from an extension group list, plus two focus group discussions, could describe practices and constraints. Analysis may use frequencies, percentages and cross-tabulations. Report the response rate and missing data. Do not claim cause and effect from a descriptive survey.

sections.heading: Attachment and report
sections.text:
Field attachment is supervised work. Plan it with your department and host organisation: agree dates, tasks, a supervisor and a logbook. Meet your supervisor and record what you did, learned and found difficult.

The reflective write-up is not a diary; it links experience to theory, ethics and your own learning. The final report follows your department’s structure and referencing style. Cite every borrowed idea in the text and give full details in the references. Check the departmental guide, because formats vary.

keyPoints: A project problem should be specific, evidence-based and useful to farmers or an extension service.
Objectives should be measurable and matched to the methods.
The literature review should link sources to the problem and end with a clear gap.
Methodology must describe sampling, instruments, data collection and analysis honestly.
Field attachment needs agreed tasks, a supervisor and a logbook.
Reports must follow the department’s structure and cite all borrowed ideas.

en.title: Advanced Theory and Policy of Agricultural Advisory Services
en.short: Competing extension theories, pluralism, privatisation, decentralisation and cross-country evidence.

sections.heading: Competing theories
sections.text: Extension theory answers three questions: who is the client, what counts as success, and who pays. The technology transfer view treats extension as a linear bridge from research to farmers; success is adoption. The adult education view treats farmers as learners and citizens; success is critical thinking and collective action. Demand-led or market-led views treat advisory services as a service that farmers or value chains pay for; success is client satisfaction and commercial benefit. Innovation systems views stress that knowledge is co-produced among many actors, not only research and extension. These theories compete because each favours different clients, methods and accountability.

sections.heading: Policy frameworks
sections.text: Public provision means government funds and runs the service. Pluralism means several providers, public, private, NGO and farmer organisations, operate together, often with coordination or vouchers. Privatisation shifts ownership or funding to firms or fee-paying clients. Decentralisation moves decisions and budgets to local government or district bodies. Each has trade-offs. Pluralism can widen choice but risks fragmentation. Privatisation can improve responsiveness but may neglect public goods and poor farmers. Decentralisation can fit local priorities but needs local capacity, clear funding and accountability. Policy must decide which services are public goods, such as advice on soil and water conservation or market information, and which can be charged for.

sections.heading: Country comparison and evidence
sections.text: Countries combine these frameworks differently. The Netherlands moved much public extension to private advisory firms in the 1990s. Uganda’s National Agricultural Advisory Services (NAADS) used decentralised, demand-driven advisory services with contracted providers. Nigeria relies mainly on public federal, state and local extension, with growing NGO and private roles. Reviews across countries find mixed performance: no single model consistently raises yields or equity. Outcomes depend on funding, staff skills, accountability, farmer voice and whether advice fits the farm system. Illustrative case: Amina, a district officer in Uganda, contracts one NGO and two private advisers for 1,200 farmers who pay a small fee. This is pluralistic and decentralised. If fees exclude poorer farmers, the council can fund group advice or vouchers.

keyPoints: Extension theory shapes who is served, what success means and who pays.
Pluralism means several providers, public and private, serve farmers together.
Privatisation can improve responsiveness but may exclude poor farmers without public funding.
Decentralisation can fit local needs but requires local capacity and clear budgets.
Cross-country evidence is mixed; no single advisory model performs best everywhere.
Policy should fund public-good advice and monitor equity and performance.

en.title: Agricultural Innovation Systems and Scaling of Impact
en.short: Innovation systems actors and links, theories of change, scaling pathways, reach, adoption and impact.

sections.heading: Systems perspective
sections.text: An agricultural innovation system (AIS) is the set of actors, institutions and relationships that shape how knowledge becomes useful practice. It treats innovation as interaction, not a product passed down a line. Farmers, researchers, advisers, input suppliers, traders, processors, financiers, regulators and media all contribute. Institutions include rules, norms, markets and policies. The perspective asks whether the system supports learning and problem-solving, not only whether a technology exists.

sections.heading: Actors and links
sections.text: Actors have different roles and incentives. Farmers test and adapt; researchers generate and validate knowledge; extension and advisory services broker learning; private firms supply inputs and buy output; government sets standards. Links carry knowledge: partnerships, value chain relationships, farmer groups, ICT platforms and multi-stakeholder platforms. Boundary organisations and innovation brokers connect groups that rarely talk. Weak links leave isolated successes. A useful check is whether information, finance and feedback flow both ways.

sections.heading: Theories and scaling
sections.text: A theory of change sets out how an intervention expects to cause change: activities, outputs, outcomes, assumptions and external factors. Linear transfer assumes research produces technology and extension spreads it. Systems and participatory theories stress co-learning, local adaptation and institutional change. Scaling has pathways: scaling out to more people, scaling up through policy and institutions, and scaling deep through changed norms and relationships. A scaling pathway is the route by which a proven change is expanded and sustained.

sections.heading: Reach to impact
sections.text: Reach is the number or share exposed to an extension intervention. Adoption is use of a practice, often measured by trial, continued use and intensity. Impact is the change in welfare caused by the intervention, not just among users. Impact assessment compares outcomes with a credible counterfactual, using baselines, comparison groups or theory-based contribution analysis. Example: in Nigeria, 200 farmers attend training, 120 try a new variety and 90 continue. Reach is 200, adoption 120, sustained use 90. Impact is the yield or income difference caused, checked against non-participants.

keyPoints: An AIS treats innovation as interaction among actors, institutions and links, not a one-way transfer.
Farmers, researchers, advisers, firms, government and others have distinct roles and incentives.
Knowledge flows through partnerships, platforms, value chains and brokers; weak links limit impact.
A theory of change states activities, outcomes, assumptions and external factors.
Scaling out, up and deep are distinct pathways to wider and sustained change.
Reach counts exposure; adoption counts use; impact is the welfare change caused, judged against a counterfactual.

en.title: Advanced Research Methods and Dissertation in Extension
en.short: Qualitative, mixed and impact methods, sampling, software and the master’s dissertation path.

sections.heading: Qualitative and mixed methods
sections.text:
Qualitative research asks how and why people act. It uses interviews, focus groups, observation and case studies, often with purposive sampling, where cases are chosen for relevance, not randomness. Thematic analysis codes text, groups codes into themes and checks them against the data. Report trustworthiness: credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability.

Mixed methods combine qualitative and quantitative strands. Common designs are convergent parallel, explanatory sequential and exploratory sequential. State why mixing helps and where the strands are integrated.

sections.heading: Evaluation and sampling
sections.text:
Participatory evaluation involves stakeholders in setting questions, indicators and interpreting findings. Impact evaluation estimates a programme’s causal effect against a counterfactual, what would have happened without it. Randomised assignment gives the strongest counterfactual; quasi-experimental designs use difference-in-differences, matching or regression discontinuity. State assumptions and test them.

Sampling may be probability (random) or non-probability (purposive, quota). Define the sampling frame, the list of units. For a proportion, n = z²p(1−p) ÷ e². With p = 0.5, e = 0.05 and z = 1.96: n = 1.96² × 0.25 ÷ 0.05² = 384.16, so 385. For a finite population N = 1,200, n_adj = 385 ÷ (1 + 384 ÷ 1,200) = 292. Measurement needs validity (measures the right concept) and reliability (consistent results); watch bias, wording and scales.

sections.heading: Software and dissertation path
sections.text:
Statistical software such as R, Stata, SPSS and Python handles data cleaning, sampling weights, regression and impact estimates; qualitative software such as NVivo or ATLAS.ti supports coding. Document every step so results can be reproduced.

The dissertation starts with a proposal: problem, questions, literature, design, sample, instruments, analysis plan and timeline. Obtain ethics clearance before fieldwork: informed consent, confidentiality, risk assessment and permission for vulnerable groups. Then pilot the instruments, collect, analyse and write. The defence is a viva: present methods and findings, answer questions and revise as required.

keyPoints: Qualitative research uses purposive sampling and thematic analysis, and reports trustworthiness.
Mixed methods combine strands; state the design and the point of integration.
Impact evaluation needs a counterfactual; randomised or quasi-experimental designs estimate causal effects.
Sample size for a proportion: n = z²p(1−p) ÷ e²; adjust for a finite population with n_adj = n ÷ (1 + (n−1) ÷ N).
Validity means measuring the right concept; reliability means measuring it consistently.
The dissertation moves from proposal and ethics clearance through fieldwork and analysis to defence, documenting software steps for reproducibility.
